'''Barbara Stoddard Burks''' (December 22, 1902—May 25, 1943) was an American psychologist known for her research on the [[nature versus nurture|nature-nurture debate]] as it pertained to [[human intelligence|intelligence]] and other human traits.<ref name=science/> She has been credited with "...pioneer[ing] the statistical techniques which continue to ground the trenchant nature/nurture debates about intelligence in American psychology."<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=apknpVTaGKYC |title=Gentlemen's Disagreement: Alfred Kinsey, Lewis Terman, and the Sexual Politics of Smart Men |last=Hegarty |first=Peter |date=2013-07-02 |publisher=[[University of Chicago Press]] |isbn=9780226024615 |pages=81 |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Burks was born on December 22, 1902, in [[New York City]], [[New York (state)|New York]], to Jesse and Frances Burks. When she was a child, her family moved to many different locations before eventually settling in California. There, she started her undergraduate studies at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where she worked with [[Edward C. Tolman]]. Under Tolman's supervision, she became skilled at conducting statistical analyses based on his research on [[rat]] breeding. In her senior year, she transferred to [[Stanford University]], where she began studying under [[Lewis Terman]]. She received her bachelor's degree from Stanford in 1924. Terman was so impressed with her performance as an undergraduate that he recommended that she immediately enroll in graduate school. She then did exactly that, enrolling in Stanford's Ph.D. program in psychology, where she worked with Terman on his "Genetic Studies of Genius" project.<ref name=feministvoices/>

==Career==
In the early 1930s, Burks worked as a consulting psychologist at various schools in the city of [[Pasadena]], California. From 1933 to 1935, she worked at the [[Harold E. Jones Child Study Center|Institute of Child Welfare]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. In 1935, she was a member of a [[Social Science Research Council]] committee, on which she was tasked with compiling research on [[personality trait]]s relative to competition and cooperation. Also in 1935, she was given a fellowship by the [[General Education Board]] to study psychology in Europe,<ref name=ajp/> where she collaborated with [[Jean Piaget]], [[Carl Jung]], and [[Charlotte Buhler]].<ref name=feministvoices/> In 1936, she returned to the United States, where she was named a research associate at the [[Carnegie Institution for Science|Carnegie Institute of Washington]] at [[Cold Spring Harbor, New York|Cold Spring Harbor]]. While there, she was tasked with analyzing the utility of human pedigrees in the institute's Genetics Record Office. In 1938, Gordon Allport, the president of the American Psychological Association at the time, appointed her as the first secretary.<ref>{{Cite book |last=King |first=D. B. |title=Barbara Stoddard Burks: Pioneer Behavioral Geneticist and Humanitarian |year=1996 |edition=Vol. 2}}</ref> She was later made chairperson of the newly formed American Psychological Association Committee on Displaced Foreign Psychologists.<ref name=ajp/><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ABlpDQAAQBAJ |title=A Mind at Play: How Claude Shannon Invented the Information Age |last1=Soni |first1=Jimmy |last2=Goodman |first2=Rob |date=2017-07-18 |publisher=[[Simon and Schuster]] |isbn=9781476766706 |page=52 |language=en |author-link=Jimmy Soni}}</ref> She also supervised [[Claude Shannon]] during a summer research program at the Institute in 1939, where Shannon conducted the research on [[genetic algebra]] that led to his dissertation.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NQPHCQAAQBAJ |title=The Cybernetics Moment: Or Why We Call Our Age the Information Age |last=Kline |first=Ronald R. |date=2015-06-04 |publisher=[[JHU Press]] |isbn=9781421416717 |pages=28 |language=en}}</ref> Also in 1939, she was named the chairwoman of an "abnormal human characters" section meeting at the Seventh [[International Congress of Genetics]], making her one of only two women to be so named. She became a research associate at [[Columbia University]] in 1940. In 1943, she received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] for 1943–1944, but she died before her fellowship could begin.<ref name=science>{{Cite journal |last=Brehme |first=Katherine S. |author-link=Katherine Brehme Warren |date=1943-11-26 |title=Barbara Stoddard Burks |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |language=en |volume=98 |issue=2552 |pages=463–464 |doi=10.1126/science.98.2552.463 |issn=0036-8075 |pmid=17793929 |bibcode=1943Sci....98..463B |url=https://www.gwern.net/docs/history/1943-brehme.pdf}}</ref> After her death, she was named to the 1944 edition of ''[[American Men of Science]]''.<ref name=feministvoices/>

==Research==
Burks is particularly known for her 1928 Ph.D. [[dissertation]], which examined the relative effects of genetics and environment on the [[IQ]] scores of [[foster child]]ren in California.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Burks |first=Barbara Stoddard |title=The Relative Influence of Nature and Nurture Upon Mental Development: A Comparative Study of Foster Parent-foster Child Resemblance and True Parent-true Child Resemblance |date=1928 |degree=Ph.D. |publisher=[[Stanford University]] |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u5sUAAAAIAAJ |language=en}}</ref> This dissertation, completed at [[Stanford University]], has been described as "a pioneering study in the field of [[behavioural genetics]]".<ref name="feministvoices">{{Cite web |last=Ball |first=Laura |title=Barbara Stoddard Burks |url=https://www.feministvoices.com/barbara-stoddard-burks/ |url-status=dead |access-date=2018-06-23 |website=[[Psychology's Feminist Voices]] |language=en |archive-date=2018-06-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180624035956/https://www.feministvoices.com/barbara-stoddard-burks/ }}</ref> Her dissertation concluded that between 75 and 80% of variation in IQ scores was due to genetic factors.<ref name=ajp>{{Cite journal |last1=Murphy |first1=Gardner|author-link=Gardner Murphy |last2=Cook |first2=Robert |date=1943 |title=Barbara Stoddard Burks: 1902-1943 |jstor=1417364 |journal=[[The American Journal of Psychology]] |volume=56 |issue=4 |pages=610–612 |url=https://www.gwern.net/docs/history/1943-murphy.pdf}}</ref> The data would be used by [[Sewall Wright]] for [[Path analysis (statistics)|path analysis]] of heritability issues.<ref>Wright 1931, [https://www.gwern.net/docs/genetics/heritable/1931-wright.pdf "Statistical Methods in Biology"]; Wright 1934, [https://www.gwern.net/docs/statistics/1934-wright.pdf "The Method of Path Coefficients"], ''Annals of Mathematical Statistics'', 5: 161-215</ref> The study was cited favorably by [[Arthur Jensen]] in support of his hereditarian views, but it has been criticized for having a biased sample and for its limited measurements of environmental factors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goldberger |first=Arthur S. |author-link=Arthur Goldberger |date=January 1976 |title=Jensen on Burks |journal=[[Educational Psychologist (journal)|Educational Psychologist]] |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=64–78 |doi=10.1080/00461527609529157 |issn=0046-1520}}</ref>

While working as a graduate student at Berkeley, she was one of Terman's research assistants on his "Genetic Studies of Genius" project from 1924 to 1929, and served as the lead author of its third volume, [https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.156439 ''The Promise of Youth: Follow-up Studies of a Thousand Gifted Children''], which was published in 1930.<ref name=feministvoices/> These studies followed up a group of children who had been identified as being highly intelligent early in life, and found that they were still exceptionally intelligent many years later.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1943/06/07/archives/the-late-dr-barbara-burks-death-of-the-brilliant-psychologist.html |title=The Late Dr. Barbara Burks; Death of the Brilliant Psychologist Regretted by Scientists |last=Woodworth |first=Robert|author-link=Robert S. Woodworth |date=1943-06-07 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=2018-06-24 |language=en}}</ref>

At the time of her death, she had recently received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] to study [[Adoption study|identical twins adopted apart]].<ref>Terman, L. (1943). "Barbara Stoddard Burks 1902-1943". ''Eugenical News'', 28, 3-5.</ref>

==Personal life==
Burks married Herman Ramsperger, a National Research Fellow in [[chemistry]] at Stanford, in 1927; they remained married until his death in 1932. In 1943, she became engaged to longtime friend Robert Cook, but she died before they could be married.<ref name=feministvoices/>

===Death===
Burks, then a research associate at Columbia University, died on May 25, 1943, when she "either fell or jumped to her death from the [[George Washington Bridge]]" in [[New York City]], [[New York (state)|New York]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=1943-05-26 |title=WOMAN DIES IN PLUNGE; Body of Ex-Research Worker Lands Under Hudson Bridge |language=en-US |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1943/05/26/archives/woman-dies-in-plunge-body-of-exresearch-worker-lands-under-hudson.html |access-date=2020-05-25 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> King et al. (1996) cite letters in the Terman archive to the effect that "She had also become engaged to marry Robert Cook but, according to her mother, had continually struggled with depression following a "severe nervous breakdown" in 1942 (Burks, F. W., 1943)."<ref>{{Cite book |last1=King |first1=D. B. |title=Portraits of pioneers in psychology |last2=Montañez-Ramírez |first2=L. M. |last3=Wertheimer |first3=M. |author-link=Michael Wertheimer (psychologist) |publisher=[[American Psychological Association]] |year=1996 |editor-last=Kimble |editor-first=G. A. |editor-link=Gregory Kimble |volume=2 |chapter=Barbara Stoddard Burks: Pioneer Behavioral Geneticist and Humanitarian |editor-last2=Boneau |editor-first2=C. A. |editor-last3=Wertheimer |editor-first3=M. |chapter-url=https://www.gwern.net/docs/genetics/heritable/1996-king.pdf}}</ref> ([[Paul J. Nahin]] has suggested that [[Vannevar Bush]]'s decision to close the [[eugenics]] program at Cold Spring Harbor in 1940, may have caused depression, which then led to suicide.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JU5dm-mOmvsC |title=The Logician and the Engineer: How George Boole and Claude Shannon Created the Information Age |last=Nahin |first=Paul J. |date=2012-10-28 |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |isbn=978-1400844654 |language=en |author-link=Paul J. Nahin|page=31}}</ref>) <!-- Nahin doesn't provide any evidence to think this, though, if you check his book... It's total speculation. -->
